title: The Linux Scheduler: a Decade of Wasted Cores
location: Section 2.2 (pp. 2-4, per-core runqueues and hierarchical load balancing) and Section 3.1 (p. 5, Group Imbalance bug)
finding: Linux uses per-core runqueues for scalability and relies on a periodic load balancer to move threads. When the balancer's load metric (average load of a scheduling group) hides an overloaded core, the invariant that no core stays idle while threads wait is broken: cores remain idle for long periods while other runqueues hold several runnable threads, causing up to many-fold slowdowns.
link_to_experiment: Our per_core policy is per-core runqueues with NO balancer at all, i.e. the worst case of the Group Imbalance situation. With skewed placement (9 of 12 jobs on core 0) we expect exactly this 'wasted cores' effect: cores 1-3 idle while core 0's queue is long. K01 (C01 vs C02) measures how much avg_response and makespan grow for per_core when placement becomes skewed, while global (work-conserving) should not change.

title: Using Processor-Cache Affinity Information in Shared-Memory Multiprocessor Scheduling
location: IEEE TPDS 4(2), pp. 131-143; Sections on the cache-reload model and the comparison of policies from ignoring affinity to fixed processor assignment
finding: Squillante and Lazowska model a spectrum of policies from a pure shared queue (ignores affinity) to fixed assignment of tasks to processors. A task that moves to another processor pays a cache-reload transient (burst of misses). Affinity-based scheduling helps when this reload cost is large relative to the service time, but fixed assignment loses badly under load imbalance because idle processors cannot take waiting work; a small amount of affinity information is enough to get most of the benefit.
link_to_experiment: This is the exact trade-off our simulator models with migration_penalty: global is the 'ignore affinity' end and per_core is the 'fixed assignment' end. K02 (C02 vs C03) and K04 (C01 vs C05) raise the migration penalty from 0 to 4 to see whether a high reload cost makes global lose its advantage, and whether this depends on load imbalance (skewed vs balanced placement).

title: Linux Scheduler Domains
location: Scheduler Domains page: description of sched domains/groups, periodic rebalancing (rebalance_domains) and per-domain flags/balance intervals
finding: Each CPU has its own runqueue; load balancing is done inside a hierarchy of scheduling domains (e.g. SMT siblings, cores sharing a cache, NUMA nodes). Balancing within lower domains is done more often and more cheaply, while balancing across higher domains is done less often because moving a task across cache or NUMA boundaries is more costly. Balancing only moves tasks when a group is found to be busier than another.
link_to_experiment: This shows that real Linux sits between our two policies: it keeps per-core queues (like per_core) but moves tasks when imbalance is detected, and it treats migration as costly. It justifies testing both placement (imbalance that a balancer would fix) and migration_penalty (the cost the domain hierarchy tries to avoid), and helps us state what our simulator leaves out (no balancer, a single flat migration cost).
